stem:
A hospital sleep service lends patients a wrist-worn sensor to record their sleep at home. On any night, the probability that the sensor fails to make a complete recording is $0.12$.

A patient wears the sensor for 14 nights. The random variable $X$ is the number of these 14 nights on which the sensor fails to make a complete recording.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one assumption, in the context of this question, that is needed for $X$ to be modelled by the distribution $\mathrm{B}(14, 0.12)$. (1)

mark_scheme.for: One correct assumption given in context, e.g. whether the sensor fails on one night is independent of whether it fails on any other night, OR the probability of the sensor failing is the same ($0.12$) on every night.
mark_scheme.notes: The answer must refer to the sensor/nights/recording. Reject answers with no context, such as 'the trials are independent' or 'there is a fixed number of trials'.

solution.working: The sensor failing on one night is independent of whether it fails on any other night (or: the probability of failure is $0.12$ on every one of the 14 nights).

hints: Think about what has to be true about the 14 nights for a binomial model to work.
Write your assumption about the sensor and the nights, not about 'trials' in general.

brisk.working: Whether the sensor fails on one night is independent of whether it fails on any other night.

every_step.working: A binomial model $\mathrm{B}(14, 0.12)$ needs each night to be a separate trial with only two outcomes: the sensor fails to make a complete recording, or it does not.
every_step.why: You start by matching the model to the situation. Each of the 14 nights is one trial, and a failure is the outcome you are counting.

every_step.working: The binomial model also needs the trials to be independent and to have the same probability of success each time.
every_step.why: These are the conditions you pick from. Choose one and put it in the context of the sensor and the nights, because a general statement like 'the trials are independent' gains nothing.

every_step.working: Assumption: whether the sensor fails on one night is independent of whether it fails on any other night.
every_step.why: You rewrite 'independent trials' using the sensor and the nights. A failure on one night then tells you nothing about the other nights.
every_step.check: The statement names the sensor, the nights and the failing, so it is in context.

every_step.working: Alternatively: the probability that the sensor fails is $0.12$ on every one of the 14 nights.
every_step.why: This is the other valid assumption, the constant probability. You only need to give one of the two.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Find

(i) $\mathrm{P}(X = 2)$,

(ii) the probability that the sensor fails to make a complete recording on more than 3 of the 14 nights.

Give each answer to 3 significant figures. (2)
hints: For (i), use the binomial probability function or your calculator's binomial pdf.
For (ii), 'more than 3' means 4 or more, so write it using $\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 3)$.

every_step.why: You are told the sensor fails with probability $0.12$ on each of 14 nights, so the number of failures follows a binomial distribution.
You choose which 2 of the 14 nights fail, then multiply by $0.12$ for each failure and $0.88$ for each of the other 12 nights.
This counts the ways of picking 2 nights from 14: $\frac{14\times 13}{2}$.
You square the probability of failure for the two failing nights.
You raise the probability of a complete recording to the power 12, one factor for each of the other nights.
every_step.check: It should be a fairly small number, since $0.88$ is raised to a large power.

every_step.why: You multiply the three parts together.
You round to 3 significant figures, as the question asks.
every_step.check: A calculator's binomial pdf with $n=14$, $p=0.12$, $x=2$ gives the same value.

every_step.why: "More than 3" covers 4 to 14 failures. It is easier to subtract the cases 0, 1, 2 and 3 from 1.
You add the probabilities of 0, 1, 2 and 3 failures, from a calculator or the formula.
You add the four values.
every_step.check: The result must be less than 1.

every_step.why: You subtract from 1 to get the probability of the remaining outcomes.
You round to 3 significant figures, as the question asks.
every_step.check: The value is small, which makes sense because the mean number of failures is only $14\times0.12=1.68$.

every_step.why: You state both answers together, each to 3 significant figures.

attempt_errors: part b: brisk: last working does not contain a value equal to answer p_exactly_2 = 0.283 (to sf-3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
A patient's recording is classed as usable if the sensor fails on at most 3 of the 14 nights. Six patients each wear a sensor for 14 nights, independently of one another.

Find the probability that all six patients have usable recordings. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (1)

mark_scheme.notes: Allow ft from their $1 - $ answer to (b)(ii), i.e. $(1 - \text{their } 0.0774)^6$, provided their probability is between 0 and 1.

hints: First find the probability that one patient's recording is usable. Part (b)(ii) will help.
The six patients are independent, and each one has to have a usable recording.

every_step.why: A recording is usable when the sensor fails on at most 3 of the 14 nights, so you need the probability that $X$ is 3 or fewer.
'At most 3' is the opposite of 'more than 3', which you found in part (b)(ii), so you subtract that from 1.
every_step.check: The two events cover every outcome, so their probabilities add to 1.

every_step.why: You put in the unrounded value from (b)(ii), about $0.0774$, and subtract it from 1.
every_step.check: A value a little below 1 is sensible because failures are unlikely.

every_step.why: The six patients are independent, so you multiply their six equal probabilities together, which is the sixth power.
You build up the power in stages to keep the arithmetic manageable.
The sixth power is the square of the cube, so you square $0.78539$.
every_step.check: Your calculator's power key should give the same value.

every_step.why: You round $0.6168\ldots$ to 3 significant figures, as the question asks.
every_step.check: The fourth digit is 8, so the third digit rounds up from 6 to 7... giving 0.617.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
After a software update, the manufacturer claims that the sensor now fails on a smaller proportion of nights. In a random sample of 60 nights with the updated sensor, it failed to make a complete recording on 3 nights.

The hypotheses $\mathrm{H}_0: p = 0.12$ and $\mathrm{H}_1: p < 0.12$ are used, where $p$ is the probability that the updated sensor fails on a night.

Use a 5% level of significance to test whether there is evidence to support the manufacturer's claim. (2)

mark_scheme.for: Uses $Y \sim \mathrm{B}(60, 0.12)$ and finds $\mathrm{P}(Y \leqslant 3) = $ awrt $0.0601$, OR finds the critical region $Y \leqslant 2$ (with $\mathrm{P}(Y \leqslant 2) = 0.0196$ and $\mathrm{P}(Y \leqslant 3) = 0.0601$).

States that $0.0601 > 0.05$ (or 3 is not in the critical region), so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$, and concludes in context: there is insufficient evidence that the update has reduced the proportion of nights on which the sensor fails.
mark_scheme.notes: The conclusion must mention the sensor/failure rate/update. Reject over-definite wording such as 'this proves the failure rate has not changed'. Depends on M1.

solution.working: $0.0601 > 0.05$, so the result is not significant and $\mathrm{H}_0$ is not rejected. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level to support the manufacturer's claim that the updated sensor fails on a smaller proportion of nights.

hints: Assume $\mathrm{H}_0$ is true, so the number of failed nights out of 60 follows $\mathrm{B}(60, 0.12)$.
$\mathrm{H}_1$ says $p < 0.12$, so work out the probability of getting 3 failures or fewer, then compare it with $0.05$.

brisk.working: $0.0601>0.05$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the update has reduced the proportion of nights the sensor fails.

every_step.why: You assume the null hypothesis is true, so the number of failures in 60 nights follows a binomial distribution with $p=0.12$.

every_step.working: Test statistic: $Y=3$, and since $\mathrm{H}_1: p<0.12$ the test is one-tailed, looking at low values
every_step.why: The claim is that failures are fewer, so you need the probability of a result as low as 3 or lower, not just exactly 3.
You split the cumulative probability into the four separate outcomes 0, 1, 2 and 3.
You evaluate each binomial probability with $\binom{60}{r}(0.12)^r(0.88)^{60-r}$, or read them from your calculator.
every_step.check: $\mathrm{P}(Y=3)\approx 0.0405$ is the largest of the four.

every_step.why: You add the four values and round to 3 significant figures. This is the p-value.
every_step.check: Calculator's binomial cumulative function with $n=60$, $p=0.12$, $x=3$ gives the same.

every_step.why: You compare the p-value with the 5% significance level. It is larger, so the result is not unusual enough.
Because the p-value is above 0.05, there is not enough evidence against $\mathrm{H}_0$.

every_step.working: There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the update has reduced the proportion of nights on which the sensor fails; $p$-value $=0.0601$
every_step.why: You state the conclusion in context, using cautious wording, since not rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ does not prove the failure rate is unchanged.

pitfalls.text: If you just write 'the trials are independent' or 'the probability is constant' without saying what they refer to, you lose the B1. Say it about this situation: whether the sensor fails on one night doesn't affect any other night.

'More than 3' means $X \geqslant 4$, so you need $1 - \mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 3)$. If you work out $1 - \mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 4)$, or $1 - \mathrm{P}(X = 3)$, you get the wrong value and lose the second B1.
A recording is usable when there are at most 3 failures, so you need $\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 3) = 0.9226$, not $\mathrm{P}(X = 3) = 0.1542$. Using $0.1542^6$ loses the B1.
If you compare $\mathrm{P}(Y = 3) = 0.0405$ with $0.05$, you will wrongly reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ and lose both marks. The test needs the tail probability $\mathrm{P}(Y \leqslant 3) = 0.0601$.

Just writing 'do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$', or claiming the result 'proves the update made no difference', loses the A1. Say there is insufficient evidence that the update has reduced the proportion of nights on which the sensor fails.

parts.label: a
answers: Each night's sensor failure is independent of other nights (constant probability 0.12 each night)
parts.working_summary: Independence of nights (and constant probability of failure) is needed for a binomial model.

parts.label: d
answers: P(X<=3)=0.0601 > 0.05, so do not reject H0: insufficient evidence to support the manufacturer's claim
parts.working_summary: Under H0, X~B(60,0.12). P(X<=3)=0.0601 which exceeds 0.05, so not significant; no evidence the failure rate has decreased.
